text: Mr. Kiley,  you want to talk to the State about webcasting?
next_text: I would. Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I'm here to present AB 816. This is a measure that would increase transparency and accountability and accessibility by closing the distance between Californians and their government. So under current law there's no requirement for state agencies, boards or commissions to allow remote access for public meetings via webcast. And this Bill would not require all of them to do so, but it would make a very important start. With every department Board or Commission of the Natural Resources Agency, and every Department Board and office of Cal EPA to live stream their public meetings. And it'll also require them to enable remote access to viewers so that folks who are watching remotely can add commentary and can interact and participate just as if they were there. The bill also requires these agencies to make webcasts available online for no less than three years. I think this is a very important measure for allowing folks who cannot necessarily come to Sacramento for a meeting, but do have an interest in the very important functions that these bodies consider. To be able to participate and to be able to be able to see what's going on. And I think it could provide a good model for continuing to make government functions more accessible to folks throughout our state. So, I respectfully ask for an aye vote, thank you.

next_text: Thank you, very much, Madam Chair and members. I'm pleased to present AB 822 which promotes the purchase of California grown agricultural products by state agencies. AB 822 would ask California to take a leadership role in promoting the purchase of high quality agricultural products by California State agencies by creating a state purchasing preference to promote California grown food and agricultural products. Over a third of the country's vegetables and two-thirds of the countries fruits are grown in California. We all know that California farmers grow healthy foods that we all need to eat more of. California spends nearly $300 million annually on food purchases, and our schools are estimated to spend between $500 to $700 million annually on direct food purchases. text: Good morning, Madame Chair, colleagues. Appreciate your consideration of AB 677, which will help to end the historic discrimination and bias that has prolonged significant disparities in education and employment outcomes for our diverse LGBT communities. This bill would require state agencies that provide education and employment-related services to collect information voluntarily provided about sexual orientation and gender identity in the regular course of demographic data collection. This data collection, in connection with the provision of government services, is critical for determining whether government is serving effectively vulnerable communities. Currently, the state collects demographic data on race, ethnicity, gender and disability on many state forums and surveys but our state has not collected any data on sexual orientation and gender identity until recently. A few years ago, all of you who were serving in 2015 voted for a bill to collect data in the health and human service context. We know from various studies, including those by the US Centers for Disease Control and the UCLA Williams Institute, that disparities impacting our LGBT communities are very real. For example in education, 8 out of 10 LGBT youth have reported being harassed in school leading to a decline in academic performance and a rise in absenteeism, dropout rates, depression, and substance abuse. In the employment context, 70% of transgender Californians are unemployed. 43% of LGBT workers have reported experiencing workplace discrimination. By collecting data, we can better understand the obstacles facing our diverse LGBT communities. And have a better direction for policies that could help to eliminate these disparities. Today we have two witnesses. Jo Michael from Equality California, and Lisa Cisneros from the California Rural Legal Assistance.

next_text: Thank you Madam Chair and colleagues. I'm excited to have the opportunity to present to you today AB 262. I want to thank you, Madam Chair, and your staff for your partnership and your work on this measure. AB 262, the Buy Clean California Act, uses the State of California's purchasing power to continue cutting the world's climate pollution. It does this in a way that acknowledges manufacturers who have invested in emissions control and innovation. Many companies in California have already invested in new technologies and practices to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. A growing number of companies around the world are making similar investment to comply with local rules and regulations and to remain competitive in a climate sensitive world. Buy Clean levels the playing field for clean manufacturers and creates powerful incentives for the entire market to reduce emissions. The State of California spends, on average, of about $10 billion a year on infrastructure. This would align California's purchasing power with our climate protection goals. I want to say that we're just proud to join companies such as Apple and Google and others, like the US Navy, that are already implementing similar buy clean programs. AB262 will demonstrate California's climate leadership and put our state's money where it's environmental values are. I respectfully ask for your aye vote and with me I have 3 witnesses. I have Mark Olson, Vice President and General Manager of Gerdau Steel of North America, Jeff Davis, Vice President and General Manager of Central Concrete, a business unit of U.S. Concrete, and I have J.B. Tengco, West Coast Director of the BlueGreen Alliance.

next_text: Madam Chair, members, it is my pleasure to present you AB77, a bill that will require major regulations with an estimated economic impact at 15 million or more, to return to the Legislature for return and approval. While these regulations are intended to carry out the policy objectives passed by the Legislature, there were concerns over a lack of transparency in establishing these regulations, especially as it relates to their economic costs. As legislators, we have a duty to ensure that all agencies receive the proper oversight. This should be a definite priority not only at this Committee but of the Legislature as a whole. text: All right, the next bill that we're going to be presenting is AB 961, AB 961 is on Consent, so then we will be presenting AB 1635. Okay. Small business procurement goals. While small business participation rates have been improving, small business groups are concerned that without codification, affirmative implementation of the small business participation goal may wane as administrators change in coming years. next_text: Good morning, Mr. Chair. We do have three bills, so I'm going to go ahead and start with AB 510, which is West Coyote Hills Open Space Project. Members, AB 510 would help save the largest remaining open space in a highly urbanized area of Orange County, and Los Angeles to be enjoyed by over 1 million people as a natural preserve. There is a great imbalance of parks and open space between North, and South County. North Orange County is highly urbanized with a few parks, and even fewer opportunities for new parks.  Comparing parks per capita between North and South Counties we see a huge disadvantage. North Orange County has one acre per 246 people, and South County has one acre per six people.  The national recreation parks Association standard for park land is one acre per 100 people within the seven miles of West Coyote Hills.  Similarly, there's over 250,000 residents in Southeast Los Angeles who live near West Coyote Hills. Basically, this open space project is a project that there has been interest in for over 25 years and as we continue to see more density that we need for homes, we know that when we've confined one space of 510 acres we want to do everything we can to preserve this space. So I would respectfully ask for an aye vote. I'd also like to let you know, that we know that there's quite a bit of work to do on this bill and we will be working within other committees to work on those.

I'd like to start off by accepting the amendments listed on page two of the analysis that provide DGS with the flexibility to cease implementing the bill if DGS determines that it cannot meet the specific talk it set out in the bill. AB 749 establishes procurement goals for the state vehicle fleet, so that by the year 2025, 15% of the new vehicles that are purchased at how the gross vehicle weight of over 19,000 pounds are zero-emission vehicles. Then by the year 2030, it will increase that percentage to 30%. In the year 2012, Governor Brown issued Executive Order B16- 2012 which call for 1.5 million zero-emission vehicles on the road in California by the year 2025 as a means of helping the state reach the greenhouse gas emission reduction goals. Included in the Executive Order was a requirement that at least 25% of the fleet purchases of light, heavy, light duty vehicles be zero-emission by the year 2020. However, there is no mention of larger heavier duty vehicles. Fossil fuel trucks and buses produce disproportionately higher GHG and air pollution emissions. According to a recent report from the Union of Concerned Scientists and the Greenlining Institute, heavy duty vehicles actually account for 33% of California's smog causing nitrogen oxides, or NOx, emissions in 40% of the harmful particulate matter created by burning fossil fuels. Larger self-vehicles, trucks, and buses are being developed every single day. There are currently 14 manufacturers in this area that manufacture truck itself, trucks and buses in California. AB 739 will build on the Governor's Executive Order, and ensure that the State is doing its part to help reach GHG emission goals by increasing the number of larger ZEV within the State vehicle fleet. With that, I respectfully ask for your aye vote.

next_text: Good morning, Madame Chair and members. My name's Jason Barbosw. I'm the Western States Policy Manager with the Union of Concerned Scientists, and pleased to speak in support of AB 739 today. As many of you probably know, just last year, numerous state agencies jointly completed a sustainable freight action plan, in response to Governor Brown's 2015 Executive Order on the topic. And in that plan, the state commits to a vision of quote, transporting freight reliably and efficiently by zero-emissions equipment everywhere feasible. And near zero-emission equipment powered by clean low carbon renewable fuels everywhere else. UCF strongly supports this vision, and we see AB 739 as an important step towards making the vision a reality. Today, there is a small but growing number of electric truck options available in the market supported by incentive programs, and a growing California-base electric truck manufacturing sector. The next several years will be critical to commercializing and deploying electric technologies to ensure they are an increasingly viable option for more fleets. Specifically state purchases of heavy duty of electric technologies including battery and fuel cell technologies, Will provide an important early market for deployment. And the state deployment of these technologies is also important for demonstrating the state's commitment to meeting the climate goals, the Legislature established last year with with SB 32. I'll note that my organization also supports continued efforts to advance lower emissions technologies for diesel, natural gas trucks. Recognizing that the majority of heavy duty vehicles slowly in the state in the near future will be diesel or natural gas filled vehicles. However, we appreciate that this bill is laser-focused on zero tailpipe emission technologies. And the reason is that electric, heavy duty vehicles are a new entrant in the heavy duty market, and they face many of the challenges that any new technology faces. This bill will incorporate these technologies in the state operations and demonstrate their usefulness, which will help enable a marketplace that ultimately offers multiple technology solutions. And an expanded portfolio of zero tailpipe solutions alongside lower emission diesel and natural gas solutions. And then finally, I brought copies with me today of the Executive Summary of our analysis on the benefits and validity of heavy duty electric vehicle technologies. And I'm happy to have these distributed to Committee Members, thank you. Thank you.

And in that plan, the state commits to a vision of quote, transporting freight reliably and efficiently by zero-emissions equipment everywhere feasible. And near zero-emission equipment powered by clean low carbon renewable fuels everywhere else. UCF strongly supports this vision, and we see AB 739 as an important step towards making the vision a reality. Today, there is a small but growing number of electric truck options available in the market supported by incentive programs, and a growing California-base electric truck manufacturing sector. The next several years will be critical to commercializing and deploying electric technologies to ensure they are an increasingly viable option for more fleets. Specifically state purchases of heavy duty of electric technologies including battery and fuel cell technologies, Will provide an important early market for deployment. And the state deployment of these technologies is also important for demonstrating the state's commitment to meeting the climate goals, the Legislature established last year with with SB 32. I'll note that my organization also supports continued efforts to advance lower emissions technologies for diesel, natural gas trucks. Recognizing that the majority of heavy duty vehicles slowly in the state in the near future will be diesel or natural gas filled vehicles. However, we appreciate that this bill is laser-focused on zero tailpipe emission technologies. And the reason is that electric, heavy duty vehicles are a new entrant in the heavy duty market, and they face many of the challenges that any new technology faces. This bill will incorporate these technologies in the state operations and demonstrate their usefulness, which will help enable a marketplace that ultimately offers multiple technology solutions. And an expanded portfolio of zero tailpipe solutions alongside lower emission diesel and natural gas solutions. And then finally, I brought copies with me today of the Executive Summary of our analysis on the benefits and validity of heavy duty electric vehicle technologies. And I'm happy to have these distributed to Committee Members, thank you. Thank you.

next_text: Good morning, Madam Chair and Committee Members. My name is Shrayas Jatkar with Coalition for Clean Air, also happy to be here in support of Assembly Bill 739. I'll keep my comments short, and just want to say I support the comments that have been mentioned so far. I'll jut add that there's a great need for widespread transportation electrification to meet both our federal help-based equality goals and standards, as well as very ambitious climate change standards. So there's definitely a great need, and I think also a great benefit from accelerating the heavy duty market through the state procurement process. First, that zero mission technologies are still lagging behind the light duty sector in terms of advancement of the technology. And so this kind of procurement target really I think it will help accelerate the deployment and advance of zero-emission technology in the heavy duty sector. And we think that the State should be leading by example. And they really will be providing benefit to, not only the public sector, but also private with heavy duty vehicles in the state. And I'll also just mention two other points. One is just the cost savings that, while as noted in the Committee analysis, there is a higher upfront cost of zero-emission heavy duty vehicles, we believe that there's likely a lower total cost of ownership. And so we think that there could be cost savings for the state, and as well as private fleets once this technology becomes more wide spread. And as UCS has noted, this is also a great economic development benefit for the State of California. And of course, builds on the success that the State has achieved in doing this on the light duty side, thank you.

next_text: Thank you, Madam Chair and members. Small businesses are literally the backbone of California's economy. Over half of the workforce in California is employed by small business. Over 99% of the businesses in California are small businesses and yet California small businesses often struggle to navigate the complex regulatory framework imposed by the State of California. Therefore, this bill, AB 912, would help those small businesses by allowing state agencies, not requiring, but allowing state agencies to mitigate and reduce fines and penalties against small businesses only under a very narrowly-tailored set of circumstances. The business would have to not have a history of noncompliance. In other words, be a first-time offender. The violation would have to not be willful. The small business would have to cooperate with the investigation. And the small business would have to have a plan for mitigating the violation. If those things are true, then agencies would have the discretion to lower fines. In a response to the opposition and in an attempt to eliminate the opposition, I've taken an amendment to make it clear that the fines could be reduced, but could not be entirely eliminated. I'm proud that the California Chamber of Commerce has labeled this bill a job creator. I think it would really help the competitiveness of our small businesses and I hope it's worthy of your support, I respectfully request an aye vote.

next_text: Madam Chair and members, Micheal Young with California Labor Federation. We remain opposed to this bill, we feel that California has about 6.5 million employees that work for small businesses. That's half of California's private workforce and those workers depend on State regulators to enforce health safety and environmental protections and those state agencies have limited resources, they don't have the capacity to go out to say every single work place. They don't have the capacity to review every single thing, but what they depend on, and what our workers depend on, are responsible penalties to keep employers in line. It's kind of like the handicap situation we have now. Most people think it's unlikely you'll actually get a ticket for parking in a handicapped space, but the penalty is so severe that it dis-incentivizes people from doing it. The same thing goes for some of these labor violations. It's highly unlikely because of the lack of resources that these agencies have, that employers will actually see, actually be penalized for certain violations, but we depend on these penalties that have been vetted through this legislative process with stakeholders, with legislatures, with the community, with the public to ensure that those penalties are effective, but they also dis-incentivize employers from violating the law. What this bill essentially does is it creates a scenario where employers could effectively still be exempted from those violations. It says that you can reduce it, but reduce it to what, to 0, to $1? That's just simply too broad, especially for the large workforce we're talking about, meaning half of California's workforce. So again for those reasons we remain opposed and we understand that, and we can have a conversation about should there be mechanisms or policies or should this body dedicate resources to educating small business owners about the rules and regulations, but going the next step and saying that those small business employers shouldn't pay penalties or should pay reduced penalties is just a step too far. It leaves too many workers vulnerable, again, it disincentives those employers from following the law. So for those reasons we remain opposed.

And instead of directly contract with a DVBE or small business, provided the state receives two or more comparable quotes from DVBEs or small businesses, 8632 will raise the limit on the contract value eligible for the informal streamline procurement option from $250,000 to $500,000 for DVBEs. This increase will help DVBEs to better compete for state contracts and recognizes the efforts and sacrifices of those who have defended our country. According to the data from the State Contract and Procurement Registration system, a total of 160,143 contracts valued at under $500,000 in fiscal year 15,16 This proposed increase would only potentially impact a modest 718 that fell between the 250,000 and 500,000. This increase only affects less than one-half of 1% of the contracts state entities enter into value less than $.5 million. Though seemingly small in scale the additional 0.5% of state contracts can make a significant impact to the DVBEs who are trying to get their businesses off the ground. next_text: Thank you to the Chair, Members of the Committee, good afternoon. My name is Kathryn Lybarger. I'm the President of AFSCME 3299 Union that represents over 24,000 patient care, technical and service workers at University of California. And I'm here to speak in support of SB 574. Everyday our members work alongside thousands of low wage contingent workers who are employed by private firms on the contract with University of California. By UC's own estimates, there are more than 7,000 such workers who will be affected by this bill. Most of these workers are immigrants, they do the same jobs as our members but for a fraction of the pay and no benefits. SB 574 would not limit UC's ability to contract for services in any way. Instead, it would require the contractors that UC hires to not undercut the total compensation of UC employees as the Senator spoke about. This is not a radical idea, contractors for the state, our K-12 system, and California community colleges are already held to these standards. The Legislature passed a similar measure, SB 959, last year. And while we wait for the audit that the Senator spoke of, there are several facts that we already know, which underscore the importance of SB 574. As UC has increased enrollment and brought hundreds of new facilities online, it has increased its use of private contractors for front line service and patient care services by at least 50% since 2011. According to UCs own estimates of this bill, the University now has more low wage contractors than directly employed service workers. The UC is one of our states largest economic engines. Its contracting standards should not be creating more poverty, more reliance on Medicaid and more exploitation of immigrant communities. But that is precisely what is happening. And that's why we're so grateful for this Committee's steadfast support for these modest reforms and why we request your aye vote on SB 574, thank you.

text: SB 498, I refer to as Jump Start, electrifying California's fleets. California's got some ambitious goals around the transportation of electrification. And of course as I think all of you are quite aware if we succeed in that goal, then we have addressed many of our serious air quality issues, since a good deal of the air pollution that our community suffers from is due to mobile sources. We also utilize the electricity that the state is now generating from renewable sources, so there's a lot of advantages to doing that, but you and I don't buy cars very frequently, individuals, so how are you really going to get the kind of market share that we hope to see with electric vehicles and how do we send the kind of market measure to vehicle manufacturers, that California is really a player in this? Fleet vehicles are a great source for that, because fleet owners obviously change vehicles faster, they tend to have more miles on them, so they will buy more frequently and the other advantage of fleet vehicles is, I'm sure you've heard of this notion of vehicle to grid integration, anyway, the point being that a EV is a storage unit. And if you can coordinate when it is charged, you can use it as a grid asset. Now each of you and I individually trying to coordinate the charging of our vehicles, while it's conceivable, lot more difficult. Whereas many fleet owners have their vehicles in a single location, that's a little easier. Not 100% slam dunk, but easier. So that's the purpose of this bill and it builds on an executive order that the Governor enacted a couple years ago. It expands it a bit and it asks ARB to look at what type of programs and offerings can they give to private sector fleet owners to help us achieve this goal. So now I have my witnesses speak in support.

We ask for your support.
